title: The Grand Trunk Road

verified.text: The Grand Trunk Road is one of Asia's oldest and longest major roads, running from Bangladesh across north India and Pakistan to Kabul in Afghanistan.
An early form of the route existed in the Mauryan Empire, around the 3rd century BCE, as the northern trade route called the Uttarapath.
In the 16th century the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri rebuilt and extended the road, which was then called Sadak-e-Azam.
Sher Shah Suri ruled north India from 1540 to 1545.
Along the road Sher Shah built sarais (rest houses for travellers) at regular intervals, dug wells and planted shade trees.
The sarais also served as stations for a horse-mounted postal and news service.
The Mughal emperors kept the road in use and marked distances with tall pillars called kos minars.
In the 19th century the British rebuilt it as a metalled road and named it the Grand Trunk Road.
Rudyard Kipling described the road in his novel Kim as a river of life.
Today large parts of the old route are national highways in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

knownErrors.text: Akbar built the Grand Trunk Road
knownErrors.correction: Sher Shah Suri rebuilt and extended the road in the 16th century; the Mughals later maintained it.
